extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, journalism students, and media trainers
extracted.subtask_description: A concise list of typical newsworthiness criteria used by journalists and editors to decide which events become news stories and how prominently to cover them. Intended for newsroom decision-making and journalism training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more people involved in an event, the stronger the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include protests and tax increases affecting most citizens; emphasizes scale of effect as a determinant of newsworthiness — larger impact increases the story's strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent events are newsworthy; the appropriate time horizon depends on the medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides medium-specific guidance: TV news = past half-hour; monthly magazine = past 30 days. Stresses that recency is relative to the outlet's publication/broadcast cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known people and famous locations attract media attention even for trivial actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that audiences feel personal connections to prominent figures/places, which increases interest; prominence can make otherwise minor events newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity (Closer to Home)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that regional media prioritize stories within their broadcast areas — geographic closeness increases relevance and likelihood of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories involving disputes, violence, or tragedy generate interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames conflict as attention-driving content; includes a range of contentious events (political disputes, physical violence, tragic incidents) as examples that typically attract coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual or bizarre events deviating from norms are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarized by the aphorism: "Dog bites man is not news. Man bites dog is." Emphasizes novelty and surprise as value drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency / Trending
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories already under public spotlight gain newsworthiness through social media and contemporary relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that being topical or part of an ongoing conversation (trending topics) increases a story's news value; social media attention amplifies currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers stories about emotions and personal concerns (health, housing, work) and relatable individual experiences; stresses emotional resonance and relatability as reasons audiences engage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity / Multiple Values Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories satisfying multiple news values have greater newsworthiness than those meeting only one criterion (additivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key principle: the more of these values a story meets, the stronger its case for prominent coverage. Encourages editors/reporters to assess combinations of values when prioritizing stories.
